title-group.article-title: Validating Direct-Mass Spectrometry Screening for Grease-proofers Containing the 6:2 Fluorotelomer Alcohol in Fiber-Based Food Packaging

abstract.p: Recently, polymeric, PFAS-containing grease-proofers were removed from the US food contact market. Validated methods are needed to monitor removal of polymeric grease-proofers containing 6:2-fluorotelomer alcohol (6:2-FTOH) from fiber-based food packaging. Small molecule extraction methods are neither specific nor rapid enough to screen for intentional use polymers. Hydrolysis direct mass spectrometric (DART-MS) approaches have shown promise to screen for polymeric grease-proofers containing 6:2-FTOH but require method validation for regulatory implementation. A hydrolysis isotope dilution DART-MS (ID-DART-MS) method was refined to meet FDA compound identification and validation guidelines. Method validation experiments demonstrated that hydrolysable 6:2-FTOH from grease-proofers were identified across all fiber-based food packaging types with less than 5% false positive or negative rates (95% confidence), and a linear response across 4 μg/kg −130 mg/kg hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH. The method reliably identified six different fluorotelomer-containing grease-proofers with 14 minutes/sample of effort, making it fit to assess incidence and removal of these PFAS-based grease-proofers.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Fiber-based food packaging (paper, paperboard, molded fiber) has achieved some of the highest recycling and renewability rates,1, 2 but requires functionalization or treatment for use in different applications.3,4 Packaging circularity codes, legislation, and retailers are demanding testing of packaging for controversial and legacy substances.5,6 Several substances within the large group of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) have been variably authorized, limited, or banned in food packaging.7, 8 There is little agreement across jurisdictions about which PFAS, at what concentrations represent legacy or authorized uses, and what constitutes violations of various restrictions.9, 10

Fluorinated grease-proofers for fiber-based food packaging have shifted from coatings containing more persistent long-chain perfluorinated impurities (LC-PFAS) to short-chain polyfluorinated (SC-PFAS) moieties, most recently taking the form of pendant chains on polymers, such as fluorotelomer-containing acrylate (co-) polymers (FTACPs), also known as side-chain fluorinated polymers (SCFPs).11,7 After the US-FDA revoked authorization for grease-proofers containing LC-PFAS in 2016, a re-evaluation of the short-chain chemistries documented a data gap around the persistence of a particular impurity of these food contact substances (FCSs), the 6:2 fluorotelomer alcohol (6:2-FTOH, 3,3,4,4,5,5,6,6,7,7,8,8,8-tridecafluorooctan-1-ol).12-14 As evidence gathered that the 6:2-FTOH half-life in rodents was comparable to some LC-PFAS,15, 16 some coatings that included this chemistry were reported to no longer be sold in the US. Other coatings manufacturers began commitments with the FDA to phase-out their FCSs containing 6:2-FTOH for sale in the US.12 In January 2024, the manufacturers of 6:2-FTOH-containing grease-proofers reported ending sales of their products into the US food contact market.12 In January 2025, the US-FDA announced the end of sales for all PFAS-based grease-proofers, which included the grease-proofers containing 6:2-FTOH as well as other PFAS-based grease-proofers sold in the US food contact market. In addition, FDA revoked authorizations for all PFAS-based grease-proofers based on abandonment.12, 17 During these transitions, there came a need to track these phase-outs and market shifts with analysis of grease-proofed packaging, specifically 6:2-FTOH-containing acrylate and methacrylate (co-)polymers (C6-FTACPs). Ongoing efforts to track environmental and post-consumer PFAS also require validated methods to conclusively identify sources, historical and present.

Just as fluorine-based testing of paper is not specific to polyfluorinated coatings,18 similarly small molecule extraction methods are not necessarily fit to reliably identify FTACP coatings or track their incidence in the market.19-21 These polymeric, fluorotelomer-containing coatings extensively hydrogen-bond these polymers to cellulose fibers, and resist water, oil, and grease.11 Thus, it is unsurprising that liquid extraction-based methods struggle to analyze these polymeric coatings.22 Surface spectroscopy techniques have also been used to study paper coatings and PFAS, but struggle with feature overlap from the paper and adjuvant materials.23 Reliable FTIR identification of fluorinated coatings on retail fiber-based packaging has remained challenging.24

It has long been demonstrated that reactive degradation, or controlled depolymerization is an effective way to deformulate or study polymers.25-27 Previous studies have shown that FTACPs, as polyesters, can be base-hydrolyzed to liberate their pendant side chains.28-32 In the case of C6-FTACPs, the 6:2-FTOH can be cleaved.29, 32 Prior works have quantified 6:2-FTOH from coated fabric and packaging before and after hydrolysis, demonstrating large FTOH releases after hydrolysis.29-31 These studies have utilized hydrolysis/extraction GC-MS methods with fair success, but those methods required extensive and duplicate sample preparation, including solvent switching, and non-trivial analysis times and analyst efforts. Such approaches would be difficult for large surveys and the simple sample preparation needed for regulatory analysis.

Our prior work demonstrated that because the C6-FTACPs were used at ~0.1-0.4% weight, and because hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH is easily volatilized and ionized by DART-MS, a screening method did not need duplicate, extensive sample preparation, solvent switching, or even chromatography to detect 6:2-FTOH hydrolyzed from polymers on fiber-based packaging.32 It was shown that DART-HRMS of the headspace above a papers’ base-hydrolysis solution selectively and reliably identified the hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH from grease-proofers (and not from uncoated or alternately coated papers). The addition of an isotopic internal standard was utilized to normalize for sample handling and 6:2-FTOH transfer/ionization, and thus semi-quantification from the hydrosolate was possible.32 However, regulatory and supply chain certificates require methods of analysis to be validated with demonstrated reliability and quantified, low error rates.

Establishing or refuting intentional use of PFAS coatings in packaging is currently an analysis of significant interest.33 Unlike small molecule PFAS, intentional use of polymeric fluorinated greaseproofers on food packaging can be inferred from their polymeric status and concentrations (used at near percent-level use to achieve technical effect). The dilution and degradation inherent in recycling and paper/board manufacture (alkaline and oxidative pulping/de-inking, and large process water fractions) would dramatically decrease concentrations or depolymerize these polymeric fluorinated greaseproofers in recycling facilities/outputs. Larger or more concentrated versions of these polymers only exist in the manufacturing facilities and the intermediate technical materials prior to final technical formulation and shipment to pulp and paper manufacturers. Thus, detection of native small molecule PFAS indicator molecules is only supportive, not definitive evidence of intentional polymeric fluorinated greaseproofer use. In contrast, detection of polymeric forms in finished products can be considered intentional use.

To date, it appears direct mass spectrometric analysis of hydrolyzed food contact papers is an attractive screening technique to quickly identify C6-FTACP-coated packaging and track the incidence of 6:2-FTOH-containing grease-proofers across the marketplace.32 However, previous work was not focused on finalizing the exact method procedure to routinely screen such samples, thresholds for identifying such coatings, and compliance with needed regulatory data quality standards. A validated method was needed, with measured reliability and suitability to identify 6:2-FTOH-containing grease-proofers across numerous types of fiber packaging and coatings. Therefore, we sought to refine the hydrolysis ID-DART-MS method to FDA compound identification and method validation guidelines and examine its reliability to screen for 6:2-FTOH-containing grease-proofers across numerous coatings and fiber-based packaging types.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: Two milliliter (2 mL) BRAND ® screwtop polypropylene microcentrifuge tubes, deuterated sodium hydroxide (NaOD) solution (40 wt. % in deuterium oxide, D2O, 99 atom % deuterium, D), 99.8% per-deuterated methanol (MeOD), 1H, 1H, 2H, 2H-Perfluoro-1-octanol (6:2-FTOH, 97%), Supelco Tritipur 1N sodium hydroxide (NaOH) reagent, and LC-MS grade methanol were obtained from Sigma Aldrich (St. Louis, MO). Unlabeled (native, light) 6:2-FTOH (2-perfluorohexyl-ethanol) and doubly labeled (HvyIStd) 2-perfluorohexyl (1,1-2H2,1,2-13C2) ethanol at >99% 1,2-13C2, and 98% 1,1-D2, were both purchased as 50 μg/mL methanol solutions from Wellington Laboratories. (Guelph, Ontario). Precision NMR Sample Tubes and Solid Top Caps were obtained from New Era Enterprises Inc. (Vineland, NJ). Snap-top microcentrifuge tubes (2 mL, polypropylene) were purchased from Eppendorf (Hamburg, DE).

Twenty-four paper and fiber-based food packaging materials with known grease-proofer coatings were acquired over many years from coatings manufacturers, paper mills, and packaging manufacturers to create a unique and necessary inventory of materials with known qualities that would be required for accurate method validation; these were stored separately in two nested LDPE bags at room temperature (Table 1). Grease-proofer coating status was communicated from the source of each material and confirmed by previous studies34,35, 36 and/or hydrolysis 19F NMR analysis. Technical coatings A-F and their corresponding authorizations (6-8) were the focus of the phaseout agreements, while coatings G-J, and their previous authorizations (1-4) were already retired. Coating J (and papers) also contained a 6:2-FTOH moiety (and 8:2-FTOH and 10:2-FTOH) for technical effect and thus, despite authorizations and uses having been previously discontinued, for hydrolysis-based 6:2-FTOH testing purposes, were considered true positives (TP).

Hydrolysis Isotope Dilution-DART-MS analyses were similar to, but slightly modified from, Scholl et al. 202532. Clean techniques of fresh foil surfaces and nitrile gloves were used between samples, as well as methanol rinses (3X) of scissors/forceps/razors. For each analysis a 30 mg sample (±5%) was cut, weighed into 2 mL centrifuge tubes and 300 μL of hydrolysis/isotopic internal standard (0.25M NaOH/HvyIStd/MeOH) solution was added. The 0.25M NaOH/HvyIStd hydrolysis solution was prepared with 25% 1N NaOH, 67% MeOH, and 8% of 50 μg/mL 13C2D4-6:2-FTOH in MeOH, yielding a 4 ppm HvyIStd (H) hydrolysis solution. After hydrolysis solution addition, sample tubes were snapped or screwed shut, parafilmed, vortexed for 30 s and sonicated for 10 minutes at 35 °C (Branson Water Bath Sonicator Model 3800, St. Louis, MO, USA). Hydrolysis samples were then hydrolyzed on an orbital shaker for 16 hours at 57 °C and 1000 rotations per minute (Eppendorf Thermomixer F1.5/2 Enfield, CT). Negative controls (True Negatives, TN) were hydrolyzed paper samples without 6:2-FTOH coatings, blanks consisted of simply the HvyIStd hydrolysis solution, while double blanks were the 0.25M NaOH/75% MeOH solution without any HvyIStd.

DART-MS analysis of hydrolyzed double blanks, method blanks, and samples were conducted using a DART SVP (IonSense, Saugus, MA, USA) with source gas (He 99.999%) heated to 250 °C in negative ion mode. A Vapur DART interface (IonSense, Saugus, MA, USA) was operated at maximum membrane pump capacity and the transfer ceramic tube was positioned ~0.5 mm away from the MS capillary inlet of the attached Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Q-Exactive, Thermo-Scientific, Palm Beach, California, USA). The DART source ceramic cone was positioned on-axis and ~5 mm from the Vapur ceramic transfer tube. The MS transfer capillary was set to 250 °C, the S-lens to 50 AU, the C-trap AGC to1x106, with a 100 msec max ion fill, a 350-700 Da mass range, and resolution to 70K FWHM in negative ion mode. The spectra of TPs spiked with the HvyIDstd contained no additional ions within a +/− 15 ppm window for either of the native 6:2-FTOH’s ions (M+O2 and M-H+CO2 adducts, Sup. Figure 2); similarly, there were no ions within a 15 ppm window of the HvyIDstd’s [M+O2]•− ion (Sup. Figure 2). Therefore, the HvyIDstd ion was able to be selected as a lock mass (13C2D2-6:2-FTOH [M+O2]•−, m/z 400.02292, closest mass ±15ppm, per-spectra). Exhaust from the Vapur DART interface vacuum pump was directed into a laboratory ventilation duct.

Daily instrument quality assurance/control (QA/QCs) procedures and measures, (background signals and mass calibrations) were conducted as previously described32. Batch analysis of hydrolyzed samples always began and ended with triplicate analysis of double-blank and then HvyIStd (H)-containing method blanks, with samples randomly analyzed in-between. For each DART-HRMS analysis, hydrosolate vials were carefully opened and held 2-5 cm perpendicular from (and vertically level with) the DART outlet-MS inlet gap (Sup. Figure 1) in-order to entrain and ionize the headspace of the sample hydrosolate in the DART ionstream/MS inlet. Each analysis consisted of 20 seconds of laboratory air prior to sample un-capping, 20 seconds of headspace from the un-capped sample vial, and 20 seconds of laboratory air after the sample vial was removed and re-capped. PPE/laboratory hygiene routines included laboratory only eyewear, coats, and nitrile gloves, with glove changes between samples and between tasks/equipment, and good laboratory ventilation near the MS, hydrosolates, and positive controls. Care was taken to minimize opening and quickly re-cap hydrosolate vials.

Using Thermo Xcalibur Qualbrowser (Thermo-Fisher Scientific), sample time specific average mass spectra, extracted ion chronograms (± 5 ppm) of the 6:2-FTOH’s [M+O2]•− (C8H5F13O3, m/z 396.00366) and [M-H+CO2]− (C9H4F13O3, m/z 406.99584) ions and corresponding ions for all compounds (6:2, 8:2, 10:2-FTOH and HvyIStd, [M-H+CO2]− 13C2D2C7H2F13O3, m/z 411.015098) and their S/Nrms (Sup. Table 1) were exported to Excel. Samples’ average mass spectra (m/z, intensity), extracted ion chronograms, S/N, and their calculated isotope dilution L/H slopes (Figure 1, Table 2) were searched and regressed (respectively) in Excel to categorize each sample’s data output as matching the detection/ID criteria (Table 2) or not.

Hydrolysis-ID-DART-MS method validation experiments were conducted to measure the method performance to qualitatively identify fiber packaging’s use of 6:2-FTOH-containing polymeric grease-proofers via detection of base-hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH in the sample headspace. Specifically, method validation experiments tested method precision and accuracy through analyses of 66 true positives (TP, 6 subsamples each), 65 true negatives (TN, 5 subsamples each), and repeatability via 32 replicates. Method selectivity was tested via 32 analyses of 6 materials with 3 alternate coatings (nested within the accuracy TNs), while carryover tests involved 2 subsamples of 3 TNs processed and analyzed immediately following 3 highly coated TPs. Method ruggedness was tested via 18 replicates with 40% additional sample mass, and 18 replicates with alternate vial caps. Method minimum detectable concentration (MDC) was assessed with 65 low concentration spikes (4.16 μg 6:2-FTOH•kg−1paper) of TNs, and upper range with the standard addition quantification of the highest TP analyzed. Sensitivity was assessed with 4 standard addition spikes and 4 gravimetric TP/TN mixes of 3 TPs, covering the range of material substrates (paperboard, paper, molded fiber).

Standard addition and external calibration were assessed with a native 6:2-FTOH/isotope dilution calibration curve (2.5-2200 ng in vial) prepared identically to samples (including combined base and Heavy IDstd, hydrolysis) but using the native 6:2-FTOH standard in place of sample papers. Isotope dilution semi-quantitative analyses were conducted as described previously 32, which involved linear least squares regression (LLSR) of the native (light, L) 6:2-FTOH ion intensities (>95% of background, from sample introduction time points, Table 2) against their corresponding heavy isotope standard (H) ions’ intensities (Figure 1). Calibration curves were calculated by plotting these L/H slopes of native/Heavy IDstd ions (for each calibration solution) against the mass of native 6:2-FTOH in each calibrants’ vial. Mass of 6:2-FTOH in vials from standard additions were calculated with the average intercept from the inverse cubic, Padê1,1 and Padê2,1 regressions.37-39 Any samples’ resultant in-vial analyte mass from these calibrations could roughly estimate packaging concentrations (assuming complete hydrolysis) by subsequently normalizing to the mass of sample hydrolyzed in each vial (μg hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH•kg−1paper). This method was not validated for such estimates since it is fit for purpose as a qualitative method.

The precision, accuracy, repeatability, selectivity, ruggedness, and gravimetric sensitivity experiments took place in randomized sequence (with the exception of carryover samples) in 4 batches across 4 days, blinded with two different analysts. Standard addition, and alternate vial cap experiments were subsequent and non-randomized, non-blinded batches. All these results were used to design the minimum detectable concentration (MDC) experiment, which was, again, multi-day/analyst randomized and blinded. To test stability of DART-MS analysis from vials over time, standard addition and external calibrant vials were re-analyzed by DART-MS three or seven times each, across up to 4 days. Time points for reanalysis were selected to systematically and independently vary the time from hydrolysis, the total time a vial spent open, or the time a vial spent closed immediately prior to reanalysis to observe if they affected DART-MS response or result.

To confirm source providers’ communications about the 6:2-FTOH containing grease-proofer status of control materials, hydrolysis 19F-NMR analyses were conducted as follows. Subsamples of control materials (125 mg of paper/fiber) were added to1.5mL of 3.78 M NaOD, 75% MeOD, 25% D2O inside 2 mL microcentrifuge tubes. Tubes were capped, parafilmed, and samples vortexed, and then sonicated at 35 °C for 10 minutes. Hydrolysis took place on a heated orbital shaker (1000 RPM at 56 °C) for 16 hours. Six hundred microliters were transferred to an NMR tube. Liquid-state NMR spectra were obtained on an Agilent VNMRS600 proton/carbon optimized OneNMR probe with internal z-gradient. 19F-NMR spectra were obtained using a s2pul pulse sequence using 2000 scans, a relaxation delay of 0.1 seconds, a receiver gain of 60, a 30-degree pulse angle, and an acquisition time of 0.9 seconds. Data processing was performed using MestReNova software version 14.2.3-29241. Manual phase and multipoint baseline corrections were performed.

sec.title: Results/Discussion
sec.p: Hydrolysis ID-DART-MS chronograms, spectra, and L/H ion ratios from fiber-based packaging material samples looked nearly identical to prior work,32 and clearly differentiated true negatives (TN) spectra from true positives (TP) (Figure 1, Sup. Figure 8). DART-HRMS data criteria for identification of the hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH from samples (Table 2) were established to be in concordance with regulatory compound identification standards.40 Examination of potential criteria that could be used to distinguish true negatives from true positives included mass accuracy error, S/N, native and HvyIStd ion co-detection, & L/H ratio criteria (Table 2, Sup. Table 1). Accurate hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH detection required all six of these criteria to be met. Thresholds for the S/N, ion co-detection numbers, and L/H slope were conservatively selected based on prior work to avoid false negatives for each criterion when implemented for such a large sample set.

The hydrolysis ID-DART-MS method for hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH containing grease-proofer detection (positive status) was validated to a level 2 qualitative single laboratory (SLV) method criteria.41 This guidance provides for 95% certainty of less than 5% false positive or negative method performance when no false categorizations are observed for sample numbers greater than 65. By using the established detection criteria (Table 2), randomized blinded analysis from our single lab validation yielded no false positives or negatives in any of the >264 precision, accuracy, ruggedness, or minimum detectable concentration (MDC) analyses performed (Table 3). With no false positives or negatives, there were therefore no observed differences in method performance across repeatability, selectivity, carryover, or ruggedness analyses.

When individual 6:2-FTOH detection criterion’s performance was evaluated across the SLV samples it was observed that there was clear delineation between TP and TN samples for most criteria (Sup. Figures3-8). While very low concentration 6:2-FTOH ions were intermittently detected in the laboratory air (overlap in 6:2-FTOH ion mass error between TP and TN/Blanks, Sup. Figure 3), these transient signals were usually insufficient to meet more than one or two detection criteria. The intermittently detected 6:2-FTOH ions from background laboratory air: 1) rarely yielded 13C ions (never near theoretical ratios, Sup. Figures 4,8); 2) were only co-detected with HvyIStd ions sometimes (Sup. Figure 6); 3) rarely maximized (S/Nrms <20) during sample introduction (Sup. Figure 5); 4) their L/H regressions rarely correlated with the HvyIStd; and 5) never yielded slopes (<0.005) within a factor of 10 of TPs (Sup. Figure 7). As indicated previously, none of the blanks or TN samples met all 6 criteria (0% FP) and all TP met all 6 criteria (0% FN). The L/H slope criteria was the most meaningful single criteria for distinguishing TP from TN (Sup. Figure 7), and the 13C ion ratio criteria came closest to yielding a FN of a TP sample (Sup. Figure 4,8). Further analysis indicated the degree of 13C ion ratio deviation from theory was closely related to that ion’s intensity (Sup. Figure 8), which is in line with previous observations.42, 43 Together these results suggest that the first possible future method failures may be false negatives, and may first be observed in samples with lower 6:2-FTOH concentrations than those tested here. However, the usage of all six criteria was successful for all samples/analyses performed herein. The results also suggest that differences in L/H slopes remain the most selective criterion in differentiating papers with 6:2-FTOH containing grease-proofers from those without.

Assessment of the methods linearity and semi-quantification was conducted with external calibrations, standard addition spikes, and gravimetrically mixed TP/TN sensitivity samples. 6:2-FTOH L/H slopes of these three sample sets showed extremely similar slopes (Sup. Figure 9, Table 3), and very similar concentration estimates (Sup. Table 2). This suggests that ID-DART-MS response at these sample sizes and method conditions linearly account for differences in hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH concentrations. Because this method was developed to categorize fiber-based food packaging as using ‘fluorotelomer-containing grease-proofers’ or not, the semi-quantifications (Sup. Table 2) should not be mistaken for absolute quantifications of free or total 6:2-FTOH in the packaging materials, but rather the amount of 6:2-FTOH hydrolyzed under the methods conditions. No information is derived from these experiments as to the extent of hydrolysis and is a limitation of this validation. The unexplored extent of hydrolysis cannot prove or disprove slow or variably hydrolyzed future samples, and thus the possibility of low responding grease-proofed articles. Hypothetical low or slow extent of hydrolysis would only put this method at unexamined risk of false negatives if initial grease-proofers (and their 6:2-FTOH) concentrations were lower than those studied here and if less hydrolysis occurred than in all the analyses studied herein. However, the SLV results did not suggest any likely false negatives across a broad range of sample substrates, coatings, and concentrations.

Repeat DART-MS analysis of hydrolsolates (standard additions and calibrants) showed no change to their categorization of 6:2-FTOH-containing grease-proofer status over 4 days. Repeat ID-DART-HRMS analyses’ 6:2-FTOH L/H slopes typically remained within 10-15% relative to the initial analyses, regardless of timing or number of repeat analyses (Sup. Figure 10). Interestingly, relative L/H slopes from hydrosolates’ repeat ID-DART-HRMS analyses appeared to show minor decreases when repeated across various lengths of time and seemed to slightly decline from initial analyses’ L/H slopes with higher concentration. However, these apparent associations were entirely dependent on a single outlier (Grubbs p=1e-10), the initial analysis of the highest concentration calibrant (3.2 μg 6:2FTOH in vial). When that value was removed from the analysis, no other outliers existed, and no associations existed (Sup. Figure 10, p>0.2, lack-of-fit F-tests on individual and multiple, linear, log-linear, and quadratic least-square regressions). All repeat analyses yielded L/H slopes within <16% of initial analyses. Collectively these demonstrate hydrosolates’ ID-DART-HRMS analyses remain stable over at least 4 days.

Efforts to detect modern polymeric fluorinated greaseproofers are rare.30 Instead, many recent studies set out to detect residues of neutral, small molecule PFAS associated with greasproofers30, 44-47 (specifically fluorotelomer alcohols), or on occasion, to account for ‘PFAS precursors’30 to provide supportive evidence of intentional polymeric fluorinated greaseproofer use. While these prior works established critical understandings of the status and scale of PFAS residues (including 6:2-FTOH and sometimes in greaseproofed packaging), to our knowledge none have yet been developed or validated to specifically detect or screen for polymeric fluorinated greaseproofers, making direct method performance comparisons not feasible. Although previous studies could not know, a priori, which samples contain polymeric greaseproofers and the specific formulation, the ranges of extractable 6:2-FTOH quantified in prior packaging studies (0.5-4000 μg•kg−1) overlapped with the hydrolyzed minimum detectable concentration of this method (4.2 μg•kg−1). The large majority of these previously reported 6:2-FTOH concentrations for samples with unknown greaseproofer status ranged slightly lower, between 0.5-400 μg•kg−1 45-47, while likely fluorinated-greaseproofed packaging samples reported 1-4 mg•kg−1 6:2-FTOH residues30, 44, 46, 47. We were able to find one previous study that implemented hydrolysis on likely greaseproofed packaging, where 1-100 mg•kg−1 hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH residues30 were reported; this overlaps well with the standard addition quantified samples and upper limits established in this work (Table S2, Table 3). While these prior works (with different aims) measured different forms of fluorotelomers, the hydrolysis ID-DART-HRMS performs comparably well. The advantages here are that dual analysis, GCMS, or solvent switching is not required, resulting in a simplified analysis, decreased analyst effort, and increased throughput. Furthermore, documented polymeric fluorotelomer-containing greaseproofer articles yield mg•kg−1 hydrolyzed 6:2-FTOH residues, which are sufficiently high concentrations that many different direct mass spectrometric techniques could be equally capable of reliably screening for the use of polymeric fluorotelomer-containing greaseproofers.

While there is the potential for this technique to detect true positives (polymeric fluorotelomer containing greaseproofers) below the operationally set minimum detectable concentration (MDC) or unexplored artifacts for higher concentration samples, this was not observed within the broad diversity of samples analyzed here. The validated lower limit of detection of this method could likely be lowered, but thought should first be given to the lower limits of technical grease-proofing effect.9 The linearity experiments suggest an external calibrant could be used to estimate low concentration values, and if ‘detects’ below the current MDC are observed, a lower MDC experiment could be performed to validate the method accordingly. Any potential artifacts at higher concentrations than those observed here would need to remain a subject of future investigation. Finally, there may also be some utility in comparing the effects of hydrolysis and oxidation techniques on these polymeric greaseproofed articles, their indicator degradants (potentially a broader list of PFAS), and in assessing greaseproofers used in packaging. However, a broader PFAS degradant list (from alternate reactions) could also dilute and complicate source attribution. Nevertheless, across the range of conditions and samples tested, the described results collectively demonstrate that this ID-DART-HRMS method is fit-for-purpose. It was used to quickly and robustly screen all sorts of fiber-based food packaging to qualitatively assess their intentional use of 6:2-FTOH-containing grease-proofers with 95% certainty of <5% false positive or negative performance with our established criteria.
